passages.title: Natural Law: From Aquinas to Radbruch and Finnis
passages.passage: The natural law tradition holds that there is some necessary connection between law and morality. Thomas Aquinas distinguished four kinds of law: eternal law, the divine reason governing the universe; natural law, the participation of rational creatures in the eternal law; divine law, revealed in scripture; and human law, which is derived from natural law either as a conclusion from its precepts or as a determination of matters it leaves open. Aquinas said that an unjust human law 'seems not to be law at all' but a perversion of law; he added, however, that such a law may nonetheless bind in conscience where disobedience would cause scandal or disturbance, a qualification showing that his thesis concerns the full or focal sense of law rather than its mere social existence. John Finnis, in Natural Law and Natural Rights (1980), revived the tradition without deriving morality from metaphysics. He identifies basic goods, self-evident to practical reason, such as life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness and religion, and argues that law should be understood by its 'central case', the law of a community that effectively secures the common good with fairness. Law that fails this standard is not non-law, but a 'peripheral' case, defective as law and lacking the moral claim to obedience. Gustav Radbruch, after the Second World War, argued that where the conflict between positive law and justice reaches an intolerable degree, the statute, as 'flawed law', must yield to justice; ordinary injustice does not deprive a statute of validity, but extreme injustice does. H.L.A. Hart, a leading positivist, accepted a 'minimum content of natural law': given the human vulnerability to attack, approximate equality, limited altruism, limited resources and limited understanding and strength of will, any social order that is to survive must contain rules restraining violence, regulating property and requiring promises to be kept. Hart insisted, however, that these are contingent truisms about human nature and not a moral test of the validity of particular laws.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures Aquinas's position on an unjust human law, as presented in the passage?

options.A: It is law only if it is derived from divine law
options.B: It is not law in the full sense, though it may still bind in conscience to avoid scandal or disturbance
options.C: It is valid law but ought always to be disobeyed
options.D: It is law in every sense and binds absolutely

questions.explanation: The passage records both the 'perversion of law' claim and the qualification that the law may bind in conscience to avoid scandal; the thesis concerns the focal sense of law.

questions.question: According to Finnis, a legal system that persistently fails to secure the common good with fairness is

options.A: a peripheral case of law, defective as law and lacking the moral claim to obedience
options.B: the central case of law
options.C: valid and morally binding for that reason
options.D: not a legal system at all, in the sociological sense

questions.explanation: Finnis's 'central case' method treats failing systems as peripheral, not non-existent.

questions.question: Under the Radbruch formula as stated in the passage, which of the following statutes would most clearly lose the character of law?

options.A: A statute stripping a racial group of all legal personality and authorising its extermination
options.B: A statute imposing a harsh but arguably justifiable tax
options.C: A statute that retrospectively increases a minor fine
options.D: A statute with an ambiguous drafting error

questions.explanation: Only extreme injustice, intolerable in degree, defeats validity; ordinary injustice does not.

questions.question: Hart's 'minimum content of natural law' is best understood as

options.A: a rejection of the rule of recognition
options.B: proof that law and morality are necessarily identical
options.C: a moral test which every valid law must pass
options.D: a set of contingent facts about human nature which explain why any viable legal order contains certain basic rules

questions.explanation: The passage says Hart regarded these as contingent truisms and not a moral test of validity.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Finnis is INCORRECT on the basis of the passage?

options.A: He revived natural law without deriving morality from metaphysics
options.B: He treats basic goods as self-evident to practical reason
options.C: He rejects the idea of a 'central case' of law
options.D: He lists practical reasonableness among the basic goods

questions.explanation: Finnis's whole account of law relies on the central case; the other statements are accurate.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Hart's acceptance of a 'minimum content of natural law' does not make him a natural lawyer. Reason (R): Hart treats the minimum content as contingent facts about human nature, not as a criterion of legal validity. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The natural-law thesis concerns a necessary moral test of validity. Hart denies that; his minimum content is only a set of contingent facts, which is precisely why he remains a positivist.

passages.title: Hohfeld's Jural Relations and the Question of Legal Personality
passages.passage: Wesley Hohfeld argued that the word 'right' is used loosely for four different legal relations, and set out eight fundamental jural conceptions in two groups of correlatives and opposites. A claim-right corresponds to a duty in another: if A has a right that B pay him, B has a duty to pay. A privilege (or liberty) is the absence of a duty and has as its correlative a 'no-right' in others: A's privilege to enter his own land means that others have no right that he refrain from doing so. A power is the ability to alter legal relations, and its correlative is a liability: the promisee's power to accept an offer subjects the offeror to a liability. An immunity is freedom from the legal power of another to alter one's legal position, and its correlative is a disability. The opposites are, respectively, no-right, duty, disability and liability. Hohfeld's scheme is often applied to questions of legal personality, the capacity to bear rights and duties. A natural person is a legal person, but the law also recognises artificial or juristic persons such as corporations, idols and, in some systems, rivers. The fiction theory of Savigny treats such entities as creations of the law's imagination, whereas the realist theory of Gierke treats them as real groups with a will of their own. In Yogendra Nath Naskar v. CIT (1969), the Supreme Court held that a Hindu idol is a juristic person, with the shebait acting as manager, and in Shiromani Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee v. Som Nath Dass (2000), the same status was accorded to the Guru Granth Sahib. In 2017, the Uttarakhand High Court in Mohd. Salim v. State of Uttarakhand declared the Ganga and Yamuna to be living legal persons, in the manner of New Zealand's recognition of the Whanganui River, but the Supreme Court stayed that decision. In Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja (2014), the Court, without conferring personality, read the rights of animals into Article 21 as an expansion of the concept of life.

questions.question: In Hohfeld's scheme, the correlative of a 'power' is

options.A: a disability
options.B: a no-right
options.C: a duty
options.D: a liability

questions.explanation: Power corresponds to liability; immunity corresponds to disability.

questions.question: Parliament cannot amend the basic structure of the Constitution. In Hohfeldian terms this is best described as

options.A: a privilege of Parliament
options.B: a power of the Court to amend
options.C: a disability of Parliament, correlating to an immunity of the basic structure from amendment
options.D: a claim-right of the citizen against Parliament

questions.explanation: Absence of power in Parliament is a disability; its correlative is the immunity of the other party, here the protected basic features.

questions.question: The owner of land enters it freely, and no one else can complain. The Hohfeldian relation and its correlative are

options.A: immunity and disability
options.B: claim-right and duty
options.C: power and liability
options.D: privilege and no-right

questions.explanation: Freedom from duty to stay out is a privilege; its correlative is the no-right of others.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct on the basis of the passage?

options.A: The Supreme Court recognised a Hindu idol as a juristic person acting through the shebait, but stayed the declaration regarding the Ganga and Yamuna
options.B: Animal Welfare Board v. Nagaraja conferred legal personality on animals
options.C: The Supreme Court upheld the Uttarakhand High Court's declaration that the Ganga and Yamuna are legal persons
options.D: Gierke's theory treats juristic persons as mere fictions

questions.explanation: Naskar upheld idol personality; the Mohd. Salim decision was stayed; Nagaraja did not confer personality; Gierke's theory is the realist view.

questions.question: A promisee holds a power to accept an offer within a stipulated time. Before acceptance, the offeror's corresponding position is

options.A: a disability
options.B: an immunity
options.C: a liability
options.D: a duty

questions.explanation: The passage states that the correlative of power is liability.

questions.question: The best difference between the fiction theory and the realist theory of juristic personality is that the fiction theory

options.A: is accepted only by the Supreme Court
options.B: treats the entity as real with its own will, whereas the realist theory denies this
options.C: treats the entity's personality as a creation of law, whereas the realist theory treats the group as a real entity with a will of its own
options.D: applies only to corporations, whereas the realist theory applies only to idols

questions.explanation: Savigny sees personality as a legal fiction; Gierke sees real group personality.

passages.title: The Right to Die with Dignity: Harish Rana v. Union of India (2026)
passages.passage: Article 21 guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. In Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996), a Constitution Bench held that the right to life does not include the right to die, and upheld the penal provision against abetment of suicide, but observed that a dying person in a terminal state or a persistent vegetative state may be allowed to die a natural death, since the right to live with dignity includes the right to die with dignity at the end of life. In Aruna Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011), the Court permitted passive euthanasia, the withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, under High Court supervision, while distinguishing it from active euthanasia, which involves a positive act to end life and remains unlawful. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), a Constitution Bench recognised the right to die with dignity as part of Article 21, upheld advance medical directives, or 'living wills', and laid down a procedure involving medical boards; the procedure was simplified by the Court in January 2023. In Harish Rana v. Union of India, decided on 11 March 2026 by a Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan, the Supreme Court gave effect for the first time to this framework in an individual case. Harish Rana, who was injured in a fall in 2013, had remained in a persistent vegetative state for about thirteen years, and his parents sought permission for the withdrawal of treatment. The Delhi High Court had declined relief on the ground that he was not on mechanical life support and was able to sustain himself. The Supreme Court rejected that distinction, treating clinically assisted nutrition and hydration as a medical intervention, and permitted its withdrawal under medical supervision, on the basis of the opinions of medical boards and the best interests of the patient. The Court also waived the usual reconsideration period in the case, and observed that the matter did not create a new doctrine, but applied principles laid down in 2011, 2018 and 2023.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the holding in Gian Kaur as described in the passage?

options.A: Passive euthanasia is permitted in all cases
options.B: The right to life does not include a right to die, though the dying process may be dignified in terminal or vegetative states
options.C: Abetment of suicide is unconstitutional
options.D: The right to life includes a right to die by choice

questions.explanation: The Court rejected a right to die but observed that dying with dignity in terminal states is part of the right to live with dignity.

questions.question: The distinction between active and passive euthanasia, as drawn in Aruna Shanbaug, is that

options.A: active euthanasia is lawful if the family consents
options.B: both are unlawful
options.C: both are lawful
options.D: passive euthanasia involves withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment and is permitted under safeguards, while active euthanasia involves a positive act to end life and remains unlawful

questions.explanation: The passage records the Court's distinction.

questions.question: The reasoning of the Delhi High Court rejected by the Supreme Court in Harish Rana was that

options.A: the patient could not be allowed to die because he was not on mechanical life support and could sustain himself
options.B: medical boards had not been constituted
options.C: passive euthanasia is not recognised in India
options.D: parents have no standing

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court rejected the distinction based on absence of mechanical life support.

questions.question: In the Supreme Court's reasoning in Harish Rana, clinically assisted nutrition and hydration was treated as

options.A: a medical intervention which may be withdrawn in accordance with the framework
options.B: an unconstitutional practice
options.C: a form of active euthanasia
options.D: ordinary care which can never be withdrawn

questions.explanation: The Court treated it as a medical intervention, which brought withdrawal within passive euthanasia.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Harish Rana created an entirely new doctrine unconnected with earlier cases
options.B: Harish Rana applied the framework of Common Cause (2018), as modified in 2023, and was the first individual case in which the Court itself gave effect to it
options.C: Common Cause rejected living wills
options.D: Aruna Shanbaug permitted active euthanasia

questions.explanation: The passage records the application of the earlier principles and the first-time effect in an individual case.

questions.question: Consider the following. 1. The Court in Common Cause recognised the right to die with dignity as part of Article 21. 2. The Court in Common Cause rejected advance medical directives. 3. The procedure of Common Cause was simplified in January 2023. Which are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 appear in the passage; statement 2 is wrong because living wills were upheld.

passages.title: Menstrual Health as a Fundamental Right: Dr. Jaya Thakur v. Union of India (2026)
passages.passage: Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment in 2002, provides for free and compulsory education to children between six and fourteen years, and the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) gives effect to it. Article 14 has been interpreted to guarantee not only formal equality but substantive equality, which requires the State to take account of structural disadvantage. In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court held that dignity, bodily autonomy and privacy are facets of the right to life. In Dr. Jaya Thakur v. Union of India, decided on 30 January 2026 by a Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan, the Supreme Court considered a petition under Article 32 seeking free sanitary napkins and facilities for girls in schools. The Court held that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to menstrual health, since a life with dignity cannot be realised without privacy and bodily autonomy, and that inadequate access to menstrual hygiene management is a barrier to education which violates Article 21A and the RTE Act, as well as the principle of substantive equality under Article 14. The Court issued binding directions to all States and Union Territories to provide free biodegradable sanitary napkins to girl students, to ensure that every school has functional, hygienic, gender-segregated toilets with water, and facilities accessible to children with disabilities, and to designate officers to monitor compliance. It warned that private schools which fail to comply risk the withdrawal of recognition under the RTE Act. In September 2026, expressing dissatisfaction with compliance reports from several States, the Court directed District Education Officers to constitute teams of teachers to conduct surprise inspections of schools. The judgment is cited as an example of the Court's positive-obligation approach, under which the State must act to remove obstacles that prevent the realisation of rights.

questions.question: The Court in Dr. Jaya Thakur held menstrual health to be a facet of

options.A: Article 21 alone
options.B: the Directive Principles only
options.C: Article 21, and its denial to be a violation of Article 21A, the RTE Act and Article 14
options.D: Article 19(1)(g)

questions.explanation: The passage records all these constitutional foundations.

questions.question: The passage describes 'substantive equality' as the idea that

options.A: equality is a Directive Principle
options.B: identical treatment is always required
options.C: the State must take account of structural disadvantage while securing equality
options.D: equality applies only to economic matters

questions.explanation: The passage states that Article 14 includes substantive equality, which requires the State to consider structural disadvantage.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the directions mentioned in the passage?

options.A: Mandatory medical examination of every girl student each month
options.B: Free biodegradable sanitary napkins to girl students
options.C: Disability-accessible facilities
options.D: Functional, gender-segregated toilets with water in every school

questions.explanation: The last is not mentioned; the others are directions in the passage.

questions.question: A private unaided school refuses to install the facilities directed by the Court. The consequence indicated in the passage is

options.A: a fine of Rs 1 crore
options.B: risk of withdrawal of recognition under the RTE Act
options.C: imprisonment of the school's managers
options.D: no consequence, since it is a private body

questions.explanation: The Court warned of de-recognition.

questions.question: The 'positive-obligation approach' mentioned in the passage means that

options.A: the State merely refrains from interfering with rights
options.B: only private parties have duties
options.C: the State must take steps to remove obstacles which prevent realisation of rights
options.D: courts may not issue directions

questions.explanation: The passage describes the approach as requiring the State to act to remove obstacles.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Court treated lack of menstrual hygiene facilities as a violation of Article 21A. Reason (R): Lack of such facilities causes absenteeism and drop-out, which acts as a barrier to free and compulsory education. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Court linked the barrier to education with the violation of Article 21A and the RTE Act.

passages.title: The 'Creamy Layer' and Parental Employment: Union of India v. Rohith Nathan (2026)
passages.passage: In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), the Supreme Court upheld reservation of 27 per cent for Other Backward Classes under Article 16(4) but held that the 'creamy layer', the socially advanced among them, must be excluded. The Government implemented this through the Office Memorandum of 8 September 1993, which sets out categories of persons whose children are not entitled to the OBC benefit. These include constitutional office-holders and those in specified service categories, such as the children of Group A or Class I officers, and, under a residual category, persons whose family income from sources other than salary and agriculture exceeds a specified amount, now Rs 8 lakh per annum, subject to periodic revision. Salary and agricultural income are, under the memorandum, excluded from this income test, since the status of the service held by the parents is the principal criterion for salaried persons. A 2004 letter from the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) stated that, where equivalence between posts in public sector undertakings or private employment and government posts had not been established, the salary income of such parents would be taken into account under the income test. In Union of India v. Rohith Nathan, decided on 11 March 2026 by Justices P.S. Narasimha and R. Mahadevan, the Supreme Court held that this practice, which was applied to candidates in the Civil Services Examination, was unsustainable in law. The Court held that the creamy layer is determined by social status and not by income alone, that an executive letter of clarification cannot add a substantive condition absent from the parent policy, and that treating the children of PSU or private employees differently from the children of government employees amounts to hostile discrimination under Articles 14 and 16. Pending the determination of equivalence, only the income test excluding salary would apply to such candidates. The Court directed the authorities to issue a fresh memorandum and to accommodate candidates wrongly denied the benefit, including through supernumerary posts. In November 2026, the Court reaffirmed its decision, refusing the Union's plea that it operate only prospectively, while clarifying that it does not reopen concluded selections, though it applies to the allocation of services under the Civil Services Examination, 2025.

questions.question: The principal ground on which the 2004 DoPT letter was held unsustainable was that

options.A: an executive clarification cannot add a substantive condition not found in the parent policy, and it created hostile discrimination
options.B: it was issued by a junior officer
options.C: it applied to government employees alone
options.D: it was not published

questions.explanation: The Court held that the letter introduced a substantive condition and created discrimination under Articles 14 and 16.

questions.question: Under the 1993 Office Memorandum as described, salary income of parents is

options.A: irrelevant to all candidates
options.B: excluded from the income test, with service status being the primary criterion for salaried persons
options.C: the only criterion
options.D: always included in the income test

questions.explanation: The passage states that salary and agricultural income are excluded from the income test.

questions.question: The Court held that, pending determination of equivalence, the position of PSU and private-sector parents is that

options.A: the Government may decide arbitrarily
options.B: they are automatically in the creamy layer
options.C: they are excluded from reservation altogether
options.D: only the income test excluding salary applies

questions.explanation: The passage states this directly.

questions.question: The Court's refusal of prospective operation in November 2026 means that

options.A: the decision is wholly set aside
options.B: the March 2026 decision applies to concluded selections as well
options.C: the decision applies, though it does not reopen concluded selections, to the allocation of services under the Civil Services Examination, 2025
options.D: the decision is confined to future examinations

questions.explanation: The passage describes the clarification.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Indra Sawhney upheld 27 per cent reservation for OBCs and required exclusion of the creamy layer. 2. The Court in Rohith Nathan held that creamy layer is determined solely by income. 3. The Court directed fresh memorandum and accommodation of wrongly denied candidates. Which are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statement 2 is false: the Court held that status and not income alone is the test.

questions.question: The decision in Rohith Nathan is best described as an application of the principle that

options.A: the creamy layer principle is invalid
options.B: equals must not be treated unequally, and executive instructions must conform to the policy they implement
options.C: income is the only constitutional test of backwardness
options.D: executive instructions may override a settled policy

questions.explanation: The decision draws on Articles 14 and 16 and the limits of executive clarification.

passages.title: Amending Power and the Basic Structure: A Doctrinal Ladder
passages.passage: Article 368 confers on Parliament the power to amend the Constitution. In Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965), the Supreme Court held that an amendment under Article 368 is not 'law' within Article 13(2), and that fundamental rights could therefore be amended. In I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), by a majority of six to five, the Court overruled these decisions, held that fundamental rights are 'transcendental' and cannot be abridged by amendment, and invoked prospective overruling to save past amendments. Parliament responded with the 24th Amendment (1971), which declared that Article 13 does not apply to constitutional amendments, and the 25th Amendment. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), a thirteen-judge Bench, by a narrow majority of seven to six, upheld the 24th Amendment but held that the power to amend does not include the power to alter the 'basic structure or framework' of the Constitution; the judges differed in listing the features of the basic structure. In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), the Court applied the doctrine to strike down a clause of the 39th Amendment that exempted the election of the Prime Minister from judicial scrutiny, as violating free and fair elections, the rule of law and judicial review. After the 42nd Amendment, which sought to exclude judicial review of amendments and to give primacy to the Directive Principles, the Court in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down these provisions, holding that the limited nature of the amending power is itself a basic feature, and that the harmony between Parts III and IV is part of that structure. In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-judge Bench held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973, the date of Kesavananda, are open to challenge on the ground that they violate fundamental rights which form part of the basic structure. In Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015), the Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, holding that judicial independence, and thereby the primacy of the judiciary in appointments, is part of the basic structure.

questions.question: The Court in Golaknath employed the doctrine of prospective overruling in order to

options.A: apply its decision retrospectively to all amendments
options.B: save past amendments from invalidation while holding that fundamental rights cannot in future be abridged
options.C: strike down the 24th Amendment
options.D: overrule Kesavananda

questions.explanation: The passage states that the Court saved past amendments by prospective overruling.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the effect of the 24th Amendment as upheld in Kesavananda?

options.A: Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution without limit
options.B: Amendments are not 'law' under Article 13, but the power does not extend to altering the basic structure
options.C: Fundamental rights are absolutely unamendable
options.D: The Court lost the power of judicial review

questions.explanation: The 24th Amendment was upheld, subject to the basic structure limitation.

questions.question: In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, the clause of the 39th Amendment was struck down on the ground that it

options.A: was not passed by the requisite majority
options.B: violated free and fair elections, the rule of law and judicial review as parts of the basic structure
options.C: affected the federal structure
options.D: violated Article 21 only

questions.explanation: The passage lists the three grounds.

questions.question: The holding in Minerva Mills that 'the limited nature of the amending power is itself a basic feature' means that

options.A: Parliament cannot, by amending Article 368, enlarge its own amending power into an unlimited one
options.B: Parliament cannot amend Article 368 at all
options.C: fundamental rights prevail over Directive Principles in every case
options.D: the Constitution is unamendable

questions.explanation: Parliament cannot use its limited power to remove the limits on that power.

questions.question: A law was placed in the Ninth Schedule on 1 January 1980. On the basis of I.R. Coelho, the law

options.A: can be challenged only before the President
options.B: may be challenged for violation of fundamental rights forming part of the basic structure
options.C: is void because the Schedule is unconstitutional
options.D: is immune from all judicial review

questions.explanation: Laws placed after 24 April 1973 are open to challenge.

questions.question: Which of the following pairings of case and principle is INCORRECT?

options.A: Golaknath - fundamental rights are not amendable (later overruled)
options.B: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (2015) - judicial independence is part of the basic structure
options.C: Minerva Mills - harmony of Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure
options.D: I.R. Coelho - Ninth Schedule laws are wholly immune after Kesavananda

questions.explanation: Coelho held that Ninth Schedule laws after 24 April 1973 are subject to review.

passages.title: Federalism: Delhi's Services, Article 356 and Judicial Review
passages.passage: Article 239AA, inserted in 1991, gives the National Capital Territory of Delhi a Legislative Assembly and Council of Ministers, while providing that the Lieutenant Governor (LG) administers the territory. The Assembly may legislate on matters in the State and Concurrent Lists, except Entries 1 (public order), 2 (police) and 18 (land) of the State List. In NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018), a Constitution Bench held that the LG is bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers in matters within the Assembly's legislative competence, and may refer a matter to the President only in exceptional cases of substantial difference, not as a routine. In NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2023), another Constitution Bench held that the Delhi Government has legislative and executive control over 'services', that is, Entry 41 of the State List, except in respect of public order, police and land. The Court said that a democratically elected government must have control over the officers who implement its policies, and that the principle of collective responsibility depends on such control. Parliament then passed the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023, which created the National Capital Civil Service Authority, chaired by the Chief Minister but with two senior officials, and empowered the LG to decide in the case of difference. The challenge to this Act was referred to a larger Bench, where the argument turns on whether Parliament may, under Article 239AA(7), legislate to alter a constitutional position declared by the Court, as distinct from removing its legal basis. Federalism has also been guarded through judicial review of the use of Article 356. In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), a nine-judge Bench held that a Presidential Proclamation is subject to judicial review, at least for malafides, irrelevant considerations or absence of material, that a majority must be tested on the floor of the House and not by the Governor's subjective view, that the Assembly should not be dissolved before Parliament approves the Proclamation, and that federalism and secularism are part of the basic structure.

questions.question: According to the 2023 Constitution Bench decision, the Delhi Government's control over 'services' does not extend to

options.A: every area of administration
options.B: public order, police and land
options.C: education and health officers
options.D: Delhi's planning department

questions.explanation: The Bench excepted the three matters outside the Assembly's competence.

questions.question: In the 2018 decision, the Court held that the LG may refer a matter to the President

options.A: only in exceptional cases of substantial difference, not as a matter of routine
options.B: only for matters of police
options.C: on every difference of opinion
options.D: never

questions.explanation: The passage so states.

questions.question: Which of the following reasons for control over services by an elected government is given in the passage?

options.A: Collective responsibility depends on the government's control over those who implement its policies

passages.title: Political Funding, the Voter's Right to Know and Electoral Disqualification
passages.passage: The right to vote is a statutory right, but the right to information about candidates and political funding has been derived from Article 19(1)(a). In Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) and PUCL v. Union of India (2003), the Supreme Court held that voters have a fundamental right to know the criminal, financial and educational antecedents of candidates, since an informed choice is essential to democracy. In PUCL v. Union of India (2013), the Court directed the Election Commission to provide the option 'None of the Above' (NOTA) on voting machines, as an expression of the negative vote under Article 19(1)(a), though a NOTA majority does not, under the present law, result in a fresh election. In Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013), the Court struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which had allowed a convicted legislator to continue in office pending appeal, so that a legislator convicted of an offence carrying a sentence of two years or more is disqualified on the date of conviction. In Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (February 2024), a Constitution Bench held unanimously that the Electoral Bond Scheme was unconstitutional. The Scheme allowed donors to purchase bonds from the State Bank of India and give them to political parties, without disclosing the donor's name to the public. The Court held that political contributions are linked with political choices and that voters have a right to information about funding to prevent 'quid pro quo' arrangements; that anonymity could not be justified by the donor's right to privacy, since a less restrictive means was available, which would serve the purpose of curbing black money; and that the related amendments to the Representation of the People Act, the Income-tax Act and the Companies Act, including the removal of the cap on corporate donations and of the requirement to disclose party-wise contributions, were unconstitutional. The Court directed the State Bank to disclose the details of purchases and redemptions to the Election Commission for publication.

questions.question: The voter's right to know the antecedents of candidates was derived by the Supreme Court from

options.A: Article 32
options.B: Article 19(1)(a)
options.C: Article 324
options.D: Article 326 alone

options.D: The candidate with the next highest votes is declared elected

questions.explanation: The passage states that NOTA does not lead to a fresh election.

questions.question: After Lily Thomas, a legislator convicted of an offence and sentenced to two years or more is

options.A: entitled to continue in office pending appeal
options.B: disqualified only after the appeal is dismissed
options.C: disqualified only after six years
options.D: disqualified from the date of conviction

questions.explanation: Section 8(4), which protected such legislators, was struck down.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a ground relied upon by the Court in holding the Electoral Bond Scheme unconstitutional?

options.A: The voter's right to information about political funding
options.B: Existence of a less restrictive means to curb black money
options.C: The possibility of quid pro quo arrangements
options.D: The Scheme violated Article 25

questions.explanation: Article 25 was not part of the reasoning.

questions.question: The Court's reasoning on donor anonymity can best be described as that

options.A: only corporate donors are protected
options.B: donors have no privacy rights
options.C: donor privacy is absolute
options.D: privacy of the donor cannot justify anonymity because a less restrictive means to serve the purpose existed, and the voter's right to know outweighs it

questions.explanation: This is the proportionality-type reasoning stated in the passage.

questions.question: Consider the following. 1. The Court directed disclosure of the details of bond purchases and redemptions to the Election Commission. 2. The Court upheld the removal of the cap on corporate donations. 3. The decision was by a Constitution Bench. Which are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: The Court struck down the removal of the cap; statements 1 and 3 are correct.

passages.title: Anticipatory Bail, Default Bail and the Limits of Custodial Investigation
passages.passage: Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, now Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), empowers the High Court and the Court of Session to grant anticipatory bail to a person who apprehends arrest for a non-bailable offence. In Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab (1980), a Constitution Bench held that the power is not to be hedged by rigid conditions, such as a time limit, and must be exercised in the light of the facts of each case, in aid of Article 21. In Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2020), another Constitution Bench held that anticipatory bail need not be limited in time and may continue until the end of the trial, unless the court, for reasons, limits it, and that it does not automatically end upon the summoning of the accused or the filing of the charge-sheet. Default bail is a different right. Under the proviso to Section 167(2) CrPC (now Section 187 BNSS), if the investigation is not completed within sixty or ninety days, depending upon the offence, the accused 'shall be released on bail', and the right is considered indefeasible. In Uday Mohanlal Acharya v. State of Maharashtra (2001), the Court held that the right must be exercised by the accused before the charge-sheet is filed, and cannot be claimed once the charge-sheet has been filed. In Ritu Chhabaria v. Union of India (2023), the Court held that the investigating agency cannot defeat default bail by filing an incomplete charge-sheet, or a 'preliminary' one, while the investigation is continuing, and that further investigation under Section 173(8) is not a licence to withhold the completed charge-sheet. In Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014), the Court directed that, in offences punishable with imprisonment up to seven years, arrest should not be automatic, and that the police should issue a notice of appearance, giving reasons for arrest, a safeguard now embedded in the BNSS. In Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022), the Court classified offences for the grant of bail, and urged the legislature to consider a separate Bail Act.

questions.question: The holding in Sushila Aggarwal on the duration of anticipatory bail is that it

options.A: ends on the summoning of the accused
options.B: ends on the filing of the charge-sheet
options.C: must be limited to a fixed number of days
options.D: may continue until the end of the trial unless the court limits it for reasons

questions.explanation: The passage so states.

questions.question: Default bail under Section 167(2) is described as indefeasible, which means that

options.A: it is lost if the accused does not apply within one day
options.B: it can be claimed at any time, even after the charge-sheet
options.C: the court has full discretion to deny it
options.D: the right arises when the investigation is not completed within the statutory period and must be exercised before the charge-sheet is filed

questions.explanation: Uday Mohanlal Acharya requires the accused to apply before the charge-sheet is filed.

questions.question: The investigating agency files an unsigned, incomplete 'preliminary' charge-sheet on the 89th day in a case where the period is ninety days, to avoid default bail. According to Ritu Chhabaria, this

options.A: defeats the right to default bail
options.B: gives the court no power to grant bail
options.C: makes the arrest illegal ab initio
options.D: cannot defeat the right to default bail

questions.explanation: An incomplete charge-sheet cannot be used to defeat default bail.

questions.question: In Arnesh Kumar, the Court's direction concerned offences punishable with imprisonment

options.A: up to ten years
options.B: up to seven years
options.C: for life
options.D: up to three years

questions.explanation: The passage specifies seven years.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia held that anticipatory bail must always be limited in time
options.B: Satender Kumar Antil urged the legislature to consider a separate Bail Act
options.C: Default bail is available only in cases of offences punishable by death
options.D: Anticipatory bail is a form of default bail

questions.explanation: The passage records the Antil suggestion; the other statements are incorrect.

questions.question: Consider the following. 1. Anticipatory bail is granted to a person who apprehends arrest. 2. Default bail arises from the failure to complete investigation within the statutory time. 3. Anticipatory bail and default bail are the same remedy. Which are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: The passage treats them as distinct remedies.

passages.title: Consent, Marital Exception and the Law of Sexual Offences
passages.passage: Section 63 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) defines rape, replacing Section 375 of the Indian Penal Code. A man commits rape if he has sexual intercourse with a woman in any of seven descriptions, including against her will, without her consent, with consent obtained by putting her in fear of death or hurt, with consent given under a misconception that he is her husband, or when she is under eighteen years of age, with or without her consent. The Explanation states that consent means an unequivocal voluntary agreement, communicated by words, gestures or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication, though the absence of physical resistance does not by itself imply consent. Exception 2 provides that sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under eighteen years of age, is not rape. In Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court read down the exception, which at the time referred to a wife under fifteen, so that intercourse with a wife under eighteen is rape, in order to harmonise it with the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 and the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act. The Court declined to decide on the exception for adult wives. A challenge to the marital exception for adult wives, brought on the ground of Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21, resulted in a split verdict in the Delhi High Court in 2022, and an appeal has been pending before the Supreme Court; the Union has argued that the question involves social and family considerations best left to Parliament and that other remedies exist, including for cruelty. Section 69 of the BNS separately penalises sexual intercourse by deceitful means, including a false promise to marry, with imprisonment up to ten years; the Supreme Court has held, in decisions such as Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v. State of Maharashtra (2019), that a breach of promise to marry is not a false promise unless the promise was made with no intention of keeping it at the outset and was the cause of the consent. The age of consent is eighteen years, as the law stands.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the descriptions of rape in the passage?

options.A: When she is under eighteen, with or without her consent
options.B: Against her will
options.C: With consent when she is a woman over twenty-one years of age
options.D: With consent obtained by putting her in fear of death or hurt

questions.explanation: The passage lists the other three; consent of an adult woman, validly given, does not constitute rape.

questions.question: In Independent Thought, the Supreme Court

options.A: struck down Exception 2 entirely
options.B: read down the exception so that intercourse with a wife under eighteen is rape, without deciding on adult wives
options.C: held that marital rape is an offence
options.D: upheld the exception as it stood

questions.explanation: The passage so states.

questions.question: The status of the challenge to the marital exception for adult wives is that

options.A: it was decided and the exception struck down
options.B: it was dismissed by Parliament
options.C: a split verdict in the Delhi High Court led to a pending appeal in the Supreme Court
options.D: it has been withdrawn

questions.explanation: The passage describes the split verdict and the pending appeal.

questions.question: A man promises to marry a woman, sincerely intending to do so, has intercourse with her with her consent, and later changes his mind. According to Pramod Suryabhan Pawar as described, this is

options.A: an offence of cheating by default
options.B: rape under Section 63
options.C: not an offence under Section 69 because the promise was not false at the outset
options.D: an offence under Section 69 because the promise was broken

questions.explanation: A breach of promise is not a false promise unless there was no intention at the outset.

questions.question: Under the Explanation to Section 63, the absence of physical resistance

options.A: does not by itself imply consent
options.B: is the only test of consent
options.C: implies that consent was withdrawn
options.D: amounts to consent

questions.explanation: The passage states that the absence of resistance does not by itself imply consent.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The presence of consent of a girl aged seventeen is irrelevant to the offence of rape. Reason (R): The BNS treats sexual intercourse with a woman under eighteen as rape, with or without her consent. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The age limit makes consent irrelevant.

passages.title: Principles of Environmental Jurisprudence and the Meaning of 'Forest'
passages.passage: Indian environmental jurisprudence has been built largely by the Supreme Court through Article 21, which includes the right to a pollution-free environment (Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar, 1991), read with Article 48A, which directs the State to protect the environment, and Article 51A(g), which makes protection of the environment a fundamental duty. In Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996), the Court held that the 'precautionary principle' and the 'polluter pays' principle are part of the law of the land, as essential features of sustainable development, and that the burden of proving that an activity is environmentally benign lies on the person proposing it. In Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996), the Court held that the polluter is liable not only to compensate the victims but also to bear the cost of restoring the environment, and relied on the absolute liability principle. In M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997), the Court applied the 'public trust doctrine', holding that the State holds natural resources such as rivers, forests and the seashore as a trustee for the public, and cannot allocate them to private owners for commercial use in disregard of this trust. In T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (1996), the Court held that the word 'forest' in the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 must be understood according to its dictionary meaning, so as to include all areas recorded as forest in government records, whatever the nature of the ownership, as well as areas which answer the description of forest. In 2023, Parliament amended the Act, renaming it the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, and limited its application to land notified as forest under the Indian Forest Act, or recorded as forest in government records on or after 25 October 1980, while exempting certain categories, such as linear projects within a limited distance of borders and security-related infrastructure. Challenges were made on the ground that the amendment narrowed the Godavarman definition, and in February 2024 the Supreme Court directed, as an interim measure, that the dictionary meaning of forest should continue to apply and that the State authorities should compile records of forest-like areas. The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 confers on the Tribunal jurisdiction over substantial questions relating to the environment and enables the award of relief and compensation.

questions.question: Under Vellore Citizens, the burden of proving that an activity is environmentally benign lies on

options.A: the Government in all cases
options.B: the person challenging the activity
options.C: the Tribunal
options.D: the person proposing the activity

questions.explanation: The Court reversed the burden of proof in line with the precautionary principle.

questions.question: The 'public trust doctrine' as applied in M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath means that

options.A: private persons may own rivers
options.B: only the Union may regulate natural resources
options.C: the State holds natural resources as trustee for the public and cannot allocate them for private commercial use in disregard of that trust
options.D: the State owns natural resources absolutely

questions.explanation: This is the doctrine as stated in the passage.

questions.question: The Godavarman decision interpreted 'forest' in the 1980 Act to mean

options.A: areas according to the dictionary meaning, including those recorded as forests in government records irrespective of ownership
options.B: only areas of national parks
options.C: only reserved forests
options.D: only areas notified under the Indian Forest Act

questions.explanation: The passage states the dictionary meaning approach.

questions.question: The 2023 amendment restricted the Act to land

options.A: owned by the Government
options.B: above a specific altitude
options.C: notified as forest under the Indian Forest Act or recorded as forest in government records on or after 25 October 1980, subject to certain exemptions
options.D: of any ecological value

questions.explanation: The passage describes the narrowed scope.

questions.question: The interim direction of the Supreme Court in February 2024 was that

options.A: the Godavarman case is overruled
options.B: the dictionary meaning of forest should continue to apply and States should compile records of forest-like areas, pending hearing
options.C: the Act applies only to notified forests
options.D: the 2023 amendment is void

questions.explanation: The passage so states.

questions.question: A company proposes a mining project with uncertain ecological impact. On the principles in the passage, the company

options.A: need not prove anything until harm occurs
options.B: can be held liable only for the cost of compensation to victims
options.C: is exempt because the project is commercial
options.D: bears the burden of showing that the project is environmentally benign, and, if it causes pollution, the cost of restoration

questions.explanation: Precautionary and polluter pays principles together impose the burden and restoration costs.

passages.title: Corporate Personality, Minority Protection and the Tata-Mistry Dispute
passages.passage: In Salomon v. Salomon & Co. (1897), the House of Lords held that a company, once incorporated, is a legal person distinct from its members, even if one member owns almost all the shares. The corporate veil may, however, be lifted in exceptional cases, such as fraud, sham arrangements to avoid existing obligations (Gilford Motor Co. v. Horne; Jones v. Lipman), or in tax evasion and trading with the enemy. In Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Escorts Ltd. (1986), the Supreme Court said that the veil may be lifted where the statute itself so contemplates, or where fraud or improper conduct is sought to be prevented. In Vodafone International Holdings v. Union of India (2012), the Court held that, in the absence of a sham or colourable device, the corporate structure of a transaction must be respected for tax purposes. The rule in Foss v. Harbottle provides that the proper plaintiff for a wrong done to the company is the company itself, and that the courts will not interfere with internal management where the majority can ratify an irregularity, subject to exceptions for fraud on the minority, ultra vires acts and acts requiring a special majority. Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 allow members to apply to the National Company Law Tribunal where the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to the public interest or oppressive to any member, or where there is a material change in management prejudicial to interests of the company; the Tribunal must be of the opinion that winding up would unfairly prejudice the members but that the facts justify a winding-up order on 'just and equitable' grounds. In Tata Sons Ltd. v. Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd. (2021), the Supreme Court set aside the NCLAT's order reinstating Cyrus Mistry as Executive Chairman, holding that the removal of a director, even a chairman, was not oppressive, that the Articles of Association are a contract binding the members, and that the NCLAT had no power to reinstate where relief was not sought and no case of winding-up on just and equitable grounds was made out. Section 166 of the 2013 Act codifies directors' duties, requiring good faith and acting in the best interests of the company, its employees, shareholders, community and environment.

questions.question: The ratio of Salomon v. Salomon & Co. is that

options.A: a company is the agent of its members
options.B: a company is a separate legal person distinct from its members even where one member holds almost all the shares
options.C: a company can have no liability
options.D: a one-man company is not valid

questions.explanation: The passage states the separate-personality principle.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT identified in the passage as a ground for lifting the corporate veil?

options.A: Sham arrangements to avoid existing obligations
options.B: Statutory provision itself
options.C: Fraud
options.D: Mere inconvenience of the creditors

questions.explanation: Mere inconvenience of creditors is not a ground.

questions.question: The exceptions to the rule in Foss v. Harbottle include

options.A: fraud on the minority, ultra vires acts and acts requiring a special majority
options.B: any act which the minority dislikes
options.C: only ultra vires acts
options.D: only acts of directors

questions.explanation: The passage lists these exceptions.

questions.question: In Tata Sons v. Cyrus Investments, the Supreme Court held that

options.A: private companies cannot be subject to Section 241
options.B: the removal of Mr. Mistry was oppressive and he must be reinstated
options.C: the removal was not oppressive, the Articles of Association are a binding contract, and the NCLAT could not order reinstatement in the absence of a case for just and equitable winding-up
options.D: directors cannot be removed

questions.explanation: The passage sets out the holding.

questions.question: Under Sections 241-242 as described, before the Tribunal makes an order the Tribunal must opine that

options.A: the majority is dishonest
options.B: the company has no assets
options.C: the company is insolvent
options.D: winding up would unfairly prejudice the members, though facts justify winding up on just and equitable grounds

questions.explanation: The passage states this requirement.

questions.question: A shareholder believes the directors committed a wrong against the company. Under the rule in Foss v. Harbottle, the proper plaintiff is

options.A: the auditor
options.B: the shareholder in all cases
options.C: the company, subject to exceptions such as fraud on the minority
options.D: the Registrar

questions.explanation: The proper plaintiff rule favours the company, subject to exceptions.

passages.title: Goods and Services Tax: Constitutional Scheme, Council and Credit
passages.passage: The Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016 introduced Article 246A, which empowers both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws on goods and services tax, with Parliament having exclusive power for inter-State supply, Article 269A for inter-State levy and apportionment, and Article 279A, which establishes the GST Council, composed of the Union Finance Minister, the Union Minister of State in charge of revenue, and State Ministers in charge of finance. The Council's recommendations on rates, exemptions and thresholds are made by a three-fourths majority of the weighted votes of members present and voting, with the Centre holding one-third of the weight and States together two-thirds. In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022), the Supreme Court held that the Council's recommendations are not binding on the Union and the States, but are the product of collaborative dialogue and have persuasive value, since Article 246A confers simultaneous power on both. In the 56th meeting of the Council, held in September 2025, it recommended rationalisation of the rate structure, to a two-slab system of five and eighteen per cent for most goods and services, with a special rate of forty per cent for a small number of 'sin' and luxury items; the new rates took effect on 22 September 2025, and the compensation cess was phased out for most items. Input tax credit (ITC) is central to the design of GST, which is a destination-based, multi-point tax with credit for tax paid on inputs. In Eicher Motors v. Union of India (1999), the Court held that credit once earned is a vested right, but in Jayam and Co. v. Assistant Commissioner (2016), it held that credit is a concession and not a vested right, available only in accordance with the conditions of the statute. In Safari Retreats Pvt. Ltd. v. Chief Commissioner of CGST (2024), the Court interpreted the expression 'plant or machinery' in Section 17(5)(d) of the CGST Act by the 'functionality test', so that a building may qualify as plant where it is used as a tool for rendering the taxable service, as distinct from the mere premises.

options.A: Unanimity
options.B: Three-fourths majority of weighted votes, with the Centre holding one-third and the States together two-thirds
options.C: Two-thirds majority with equal weight
options.D: Simple majority with the Centre having two-thirds weight

questions.explanation: The passage so states.

questions.question: In Mohit Minerals, the Supreme Court held that the GST Council's recommendations are

options.A: binding only on the States
options.B: binding on the Union and the States
options.C: binding only on the Union
options.D: persuasive, and not binding on the Union and the States

questions.explanation: This is the holding as stated in the passage.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct regarding the September 2025 rationalisation?

options.A: It created a two-slab structure of five and eighteen per cent for most items, with forty per cent for certain sin and luxury items
options.B: It created a single rate for all goods and services
options.C: It eliminated GST on all goods
options.D: It increased all rates to twenty-eight per cent

questions.explanation: The passage describes the new slab structure and effective date.

questions.question: The apparent difference between Eicher Motors and Jayam and Co. concerns whether input tax credit is

options.A: taxable
options.B: a vested right or a statutory concession subject to conditions
options.C: applicable only to services
options.D: available only to exporters

questions.explanation: Eicher held credit to be a vested right; Jayam held it to be a concession.

questions.question: Under the 'functionality test' in Safari Retreats, a building may be 'plant' where

options.A: it is owned by the Government
options.B: it is used merely as premises
options.C: it is above a certain height
options.D: it is used as a tool for the rendition of the taxable service, rather than as mere premises

questions.explanation: The passage states the test.

questions.question: The best reason why the Court held GST Council recommendations not binding is that

options.A: Article 246A confers simultaneous legislative power on both the Union and the States, and the system is one of collaborative federalism
options.B: Article 279A is invalid
options.C: the Council has no power over rates
options.D: the Council is not a constitutional body

questions.explanation: The Court relied on the concurrent power and collaborative dialogue.

passages.title: Anti-competitive Conduct, Dominance and the 2023 Amendments
passages.passage: The Competition Act, 2002 prohibits three categories of conduct that harm competition: anti-competitive agreements under Section 3, abuse of dominant position under Section 4, and combinations that cause or are likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition under Sections 5 and 6. Under Section 3(3), horizontal agreements between competitors on prices, output, markets or bid rigging are presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition (AAEC), and the burden is on the parties to rebut the presumption. Vertical agreements, such as tie-in arrangements, exclusive supply and resale price maintenance, are judged under Section 3(4) by a rule-of-reason analysis, which weighs the pro-competitive and anti-competitive effects. Dominance, under Section 4, is not itself an offence; abuse of dominance, including imposing unfair or discriminatory conditions, limiting production or denying market access, is. In Competition Commission of India v. Coordination Committee of Artists and Technicians (2017), the Supreme Court held that trade associations can be liable under Section 3. In Excel Crop Care v. Competition Commission of India (2017), the Court held that the penalty under Section 27 should be calculated on the 'relevant turnover', that is, the turnover from the products affected by the contravention, and not on total turnover, in line with the principle of proportionality. The Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 changed this by enabling penalties to be based on the 'global turnover' of the enterprise, introduced a deal value threshold of Rs 2,000 crore for review of combinations for transactions where the target has substantial business operations in India, introduced settlements and commitments for vertical agreements and abuse of dominance cases, and provided a 'hub and spoke' cartel concept where an enterprise not engaged in identical activity facilitates a cartel. The Commission's order against Google in the Android case (2022), imposing a penalty of about Rs 1,337 crore for abuse of dominance in the mobile operating system market, was largely upheld by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, and an appeal is before the Supreme Court.

questions.question: Under Section 3(3), horizontal agreements on prices or bid rigging are

options.A: exempt from the Act
options.B: judged under a rule of reason
options.C: lawful unless the Commission proves harm
options.D: presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition, and the parties must rebut the presumption

questions.explanation: The passage states the rebuttable presumption.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct about dominance under Section 4?

options.A: Only government entities can be dominant
options.B: Dominance is irrelevant to the Act
options.C: Being dominant is an offence
options.D: Dominance is not an offence, but abuse of dominance is

questions.explanation: The passage states that dominance is not itself an offence.

questions.question: In Excel Crop Care, the Supreme Court held that penalty should be calculated on

options.A: relevant turnover, i.e. the turnover from the products affected
options.B: total turnover
options.C: assets of the enterprise
options.D: profits of the enterprise

questions.explanation: The Court applied proportionality and relevant turnover; the 2023 Amendment now permits global turnover.

questions.question: The 2023 Amendment, in relation to the penalty, changed the position by

options.A: fixing it at Rs 1 crore
options.B: abolishing penalties
options.C: enabling the penalty to be based on global turnover

passages.title: Consumers, Product Liability and Dark Patterns
passages.passage: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA) replaced the 1986 Act and widened the scope of consumer protection. A 'consumer' is a person who buys goods or hires or avails of services for consideration, but not one who obtains them for resale or for any commercial purpose, though the Act clarifies that 'commercial purpose' does not include use by a person exclusively for earning livelihood by means of self-employment. In Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta (1994), the Supreme Court held that housing construction and development activity by a statutory body is a 'service', and in Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) the Court held that medical services, other than free service rendered to all patients, are covered. In Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G. Industrial Institute (1995), the Court explained that purchase of goods for use in a commercial activity is excluded, subject to the exception for self-employment. The Act creates the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), with power to regulate matters relating to violation of consumer rights, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements, to order recall of goods, and to impose penalties on manufacturers and endorsers. Chapter VI introduces 'product liability', making the manufacturer, service provider and seller liable for harm caused by a defective product or deficient service, subject to the defences specified. The Act also deals with 'unfair contracts', defined to include contracts which cause significant change in the rights of consumers, such as excessive security deposits or unilateral termination. In Ireo Grace Realtech v. Abhishek Khanna (2021), the Supreme Court held that one-sided clauses in a builder-buyer agreement, such as those allowing the builder to delay possession but making the buyer liable to heavy interest for delay, amount to an unfair trade practice. The Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023, identify practices such as false urgency, basket sneaking, confirm shaming, forced action and subscription traps as deceptive designs used by online platforms, which are regarded as unfair trade practices.

passages.title: Specific Performance after the 2018 Amendment
passages.passage: The Specific Relief Act, 1963 was amended in 2018 to alter the character of specific performance in India. Before the amendment, Section 10 provided that specific performance of a contract could be enforced in the discretion of the court, which was guided by Section 20; the remedy of damages was the primary relief, and specific performance an exception. After the amendment, Section 10 provides that specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court, subject to Sections 11(2), 14 and 16; the discretion has been removed, and the remedy has become the rule. Section 14 sets out the contracts not specifically enforceable, including those where compensation in money is an adequate relief, contracts which run into minute details or are dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties, contracts which are in their nature determinable, and contracts the performance of which involves the continuous duty which the court cannot supervise, subject to modifications introduced in 2018 for certain contracts for infrastructure projects. Section 16 bars relief to a person who has become incapable of performing, has violated an essential term, or who fails to aver and prove that he has performed or has always been 'ready and willing' to perform the essential terms of the contract, other than those which have been prevented or waived by the defendant. The amendment also introduced Section 20, which enables the party suffering from breach to obtain substituted performance by a third party or through his own agency at the cost of the defaulting party, after giving a written notice of thirty days; once this remedy is chosen, the party cannot claim specific performance. Section 20A bars the grant of an injunction by a court in suits involving a contract relating to an infrastructure project, where the grant would cause impediment or delay in the progress or completion of the project, and Section 20B provides for designated special courts. In Katta Sujatha Reddy v. Siddamsetty Infra Projects (2024), the Supreme Court held that the 2018 amendments are substantive in nature and apply prospectively to contracts entered into after 1 October 2018. Section 21 allows damages, with or without specific performance, and Section 38 provides for a perpetual injunction to prevent the breach of an obligation.

passages.title: Compensation for Death, Future Prospects and the Value of Homemaking
passages.passage: Compensation in motor accident claims is governed by the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. Section 166 enables a claim for compensation to be made before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, and the principle is of 'just compensation', and not a mere formula. Section 140 provides for no-fault liability, a fixed sum for death and for grievous hurt, without proof of negligence. In Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation (2009), the Supreme Court standardised the calculation in death cases: the income of the deceased is established, a deduction is made for personal expenses of the deceased, one-third where there are two or three dependants, and so on, and a multiplier is selected from a table according to the age of the deceased. In National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi (2017), a Constitution Bench held that future prospects must be added to the income of the deceased, even where he was in permanent employment or self-employed with a fixed salary, at forty per cent where the deceased was below forty years, twenty-five per cent where between forty and fifty, and ten per cent where between fifty and sixty; it also fixed conventional sums for loss of estate, funeral expenses and loss of consortium, with a ten per cent increase every three years. In respect of homemakers, the Court in Arun Kumar Agrawal v. National Insurance Co. (2010) held that the services of a homemaker, though not performed for pay, are of economic value, and in Kirti v. Oriental Insurance Co. (2021) the Court held that the notional income assigned to a homemaker should reflect the value of the work done and should not be treated as a token, since to do so would ignore the contribution of women to the household and the economy. In Shishu Pal v. Surjeet, decided on 11 June 2026, a Bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and N. Kotiswar Singh, in a motor accident compensation case, stressed the economic and social contribution of homemakers, and treated it as an element to be reflected in compensation. The Court has repeatedly said that compensation should aim at restoring the dependants to the position they would have been in had the death not occurred, as far as money can do so.

passages.title: The Right to Information: Public Authority, Exemptions and Public Interest
passages.passage: The Right to Information Act, 2005 gives effect to the right to information under Article 19(1)(a). Every citizen has the right to information held by or under the control of a 'public authority', which is defined in Section 2(h) to include bodies established by the Constitution or by law, and bodies owned, controlled or substantially financed by the appropriate Government. In Thalappalam Service Cooperative Bank v. State of Kerala (2013), the Supreme Court held that cooperative societies are not public authorities merely because they are registered under a State Act, unless they are substantially financed or controlled by the Government, and that 'substantial' financing must be a major part of the funding, not a mere token amount. The Public Information Officer must dispose of a request within thirty days, or forty-eight hours where the information concerns the life or liberty of a person (Section 7(1)). Section 8(1) contains exemptions, including information affecting sovereignty and security, information forbidden to be published by a court, information whose disclosure would endanger life, information held in a fiduciary relationship, and personal information which has no relationship to any public activity or interest or which would cause an unwarranted invasion of privacy (Section 8(1)(j)). Section 8(2) provides that, notwithstanding the exemptions, access may be allowed if the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interest. In Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v. Central Information Commissioner (2013), the Court held that service records and assessment of an employee are personal information, exempt unless a larger public interest is shown. In Reserve Bank of India v. Jayantilal N. Mistry (2015), the Court held that the regulator cannot rely on a 'fiduciary' relationship with banks to refuse information on inspection reports, since the regulator does not hold the information for the benefit of banks. In Central Public Information Officer, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019), a Constitution Bench held that the office of the Chief Justice of India is a public authority, that the right to information and judicial independence are not antagonistic, and that the balance between privacy and transparency is to be struck by applying the proportionality test and by considering the public interest in each case. Section 24 exempts specified intelligence and security organisations, except for allegations of corruption and human rights violations.

passages.title: Pleadings, Pre-institution Mediation and Summary Judgment
passages.passage: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 provides, in Section 11, that no court shall try a suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or parties under whom they claim, where the former court was competent to try the later suit and decided it finally. Order VII Rule 11 permits the rejection of a plaint where it does not disclose a cause of action, is under-valued, is insufficiently stamped, or is barred by law. In Dahiben v. Arvindbhai Kalyanji Bhanusali (2020), the Supreme Court held that, in considering an application under Order VII Rule 11, the court must examine only the plaint and the documents filed with it, and not the defence of the defendant, and that the application cannot be used to decide disputed questions of fact. The Commercial Courts Act, 2015 introduced a special procedure for 'commercial disputes' of the specified value. Section 12A makes pre-institution mediation mandatory for suits that do not contemplate urgent interim relief; in Patil Automation Pvt. Ltd. v. Rakheja Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (2022), the Supreme Court held that the requirement is mandatory, and that a plaint instituted in non-compliance is liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11, but applied the ruling prospectively from 20 August 2022. In SCG Contracts (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. K.S. Chamankar Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (2019), the Court held that the period for filing a written statement in a commercial suit, thirty days, extendable by not more than ninety days, is strictly mandatory, and that the court has no power to extend it further. Order XIII-A, inserted by the Commercial Courts Act, enables the court to give summary judgment on a claim where it considers that the claimant has no real prospect of succeeding or that the defendant has no real prospect of successfully defending the claim, and there is no other compelling reason why the claim should not be disposed of before trial. The Mediation Act, 2023 gives statutory form to mediation, provides for community mediation, and makes a mediated settlement agreement enforceable in the same manner as a judgment or decree of a court.
