passages.title: Daughters' Coparcenary Rights and the Hindu Succession Act
passages.passage: Before 2005, the Mitakshara coparcenary consisted only of male members, and a daughter was not a coparcener. The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, which substituted Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, provides that on and from 9 September 2005, the daughter of a coparcener shall, by birth, become a coparcener in her own right in the same manner as the son, with the same rights and liabilities, and may dispose of her share by testamentary disposition. The question whether the daughter's right depended on the father being alive on that date led to conflicting views. In Prakash v. Phulavati (2016), the Court held that the amendment was prospective and required that both the daughter and the father be alive on 9 September 2005, while Danamma v. Amar (2018) took a contrary view. In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), a three-judge Bench settled the law, holding that the coparcenary right accrues by birth and is not dependent upon the father being alive on 9 September 2005, since the right is by birth, though the provision is not retroactive in the sense that it does not disturb partitions or dispositions effected before 20 December 2004, which must be proved by a registered partition deed or a decree of court and not by an oral partition, except in exceptional cases. Section 14 provides that any property possessed by a female Hindu is held as her absolute property, and in V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977) the Court held that a limited estate in lieu of maintenance matured into an absolute estate. In Arunachala Gounder v. Ponnusamy (2022), the Court held that the self-acquired property of a Hindu male dying intestate, even prior to 1956, would devolve on his daughter by inheritance and not by survivorship. Under Section 15, the property of a female dying intestate devolves first upon her sons and daughters and the husband, then upon the heirs of the husband, and so on; Section 15(2) provides that property inherited from her father or mother goes, in the absence of children, to the heirs of the father, and property inherited from her husband or father-in-law goes to the heirs of the husband. In Revanasiddappa v. Mallikarjun (2023), a Bench held that children of void and voidable marriages, who are legitimate under Section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act, are entitled to the share in the parent's property, including the coparcenary property.

passages.title: Sources of International Law, Jus Cogens and Obligations Erga Omnes
passages.passage: Article 38(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice lists the sources the Court applies: international conventions establishing rules expressly recognised by the contesting States; international custom, as evidence of a general practice accepted as law; the general principles of law recognised by civilised nations; and, as subsidiary means for the determination of rules of law, judicial decisions and the teachings of the most highly qualified publicists. Customary international law requires two elements: settled state practice, which must be extensive and virtually uniform, and opinio juris, the belief that the practice is required by law. In the North Sea Continental Shelf Cases (1969), the Court held that a treaty provision may generate a customary rule, but only where it is of a fundamentally norm-creating character and has been accepted in practice, and that the passage of a short period of time is not a bar. In the Asylum Case (Colombia v. Peru) (1950), the Court held that a party relying on a regional or local custom must prove that it is constant and uniform. A State that persistently objects to an emerging custom while it is being formed is not bound by it, the 'persistent objector' rule. In Nicaragua v. United States (1986), the Court held that customary rules continue to exist alongside treaty rules with identical content and retain an independent existence. Peremptory norms, or jus cogens, are defined in Article 53 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties as norms accepted and recognised by the international community as a whole from which no derogation is permitted, and which can be modified only by a subsequent norm of the same character; a treaty in conflict with such a norm is void. In Barcelona Traction (1970), the Court distinguished obligations owed to the international community as a whole, or erga omnes, such as the prohibition of aggression and genocide, in whose protection all States have a legal interest. In the proceedings brought by South Africa against Israel under the Genocide Convention, the Court in January 2024 held that it had prima facie jurisdiction, that the rights claimed were plausible, and indicated provisional measures; the case rests on the idea that obligations under the Convention are owed erga omnes partes. Under Article 59 of the Statute, a decision of the Court has no binding force except between the parties and in respect of that particular case.

options.B: 1 and 3 only

options.D: 1, 2 and 3

passages.title: The International Criminal Court: Jurisdiction, Immunities and Cooperation
passages.passage: The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC), adopted in 1998 and in force since 2002, establishes a permanent court with jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression, the last being activated after the Kampala amendments of 2010 on conditions narrower than those for other crimes. The Court is complementary to national criminal jurisdictions: under Article 17, a case is inadmissible where it is being investigated or prosecuted by a State with jurisdiction, unless the State is unwilling or unable genuinely to do so. Under Article 12, the Court may exercise jurisdiction where the crime was committed on the territory of a State Party or by a national of a State Party, or where a non-party State has accepted the jurisdiction by declaration; under Article 13(b), the Security Council, acting under Chapter VII, may refer a situation to the Prosecutor, in which case the Court's jurisdiction extends to non-parties. Under Article 16, the Security Council may defer an investigation or prosecution for a renewable period of twelve months. Article 27 provides that the Statute applies equally to all persons without distinction based on official capacity, and that immunities attaching to the official capacity of a person, whether under national or international law, do not bar the Court's jurisdiction. Article 98, however, provides that the Court may not proceed with a request for surrender which would require a State to act inconsistently with its obligations under international law with respect to the immunities of a third State, unless that State's cooperation for waiver is obtained. In the Jordan Referral decision (2019), concerning the failure of Jordan to arrest Sudan's President Omar al-Bashir, the Appeals Chamber held that there is no rule of customary international law recognising head-of-state immunity before an international court, and that States Parties are bound to cooperate. The Court has issued arrest warrants against sitting leaders, including those against the Russian President in March 2023, and against the Israeli Prime Minister and a former Defence Minister in November 2024, which provoked debate on the effect of immunities, and in March 2025, a former Philippine President was surrendered to the Court. India, the United States and China are not parties to the Rome Statute.

questions.question: The principle of complementarity under Article 17 means that a case is inadmissible where

options.A: a State with jurisdiction is genuinely investigating or prosecuting, unless it is unwilling or unable to do so
options.B: the crime is not serious
options.C: the ICC has already tried it
options.D: the accused is a head of State

questions.explanation: The passage states the principle.

questions.question: Which of the following is a route through which the ICC may exercise jurisdiction over a national of a non-party State?

options.A: Request by any State
options.B: Referral by the General Assembly
options.C: Referral by the Security Council under Article 13(b)
options.D: Declaration of the accused

questions.explanation: The passage states that a Security Council referral extends jurisdiction to non-parties.

questions.question: Under Article 16, the Security Council may

options.A: nominate the Prosecutor
options.B: veto an arrest warrant permanently
options.C: terminate the ICC
options.D: defer an investigation or prosecution for a renewable period of twelve months

questions.explanation: The passage so states.

questions.question: The apparent tension between Articles 27 and 98 is that

options.A: Article 27 removes immunity before the ICC, while Article 98 limits the Court's request for surrender where it would require a State to violate its obligations concerning third-State immunities
options.B: both articles refer to aggression only
options.C: Article 98 abolishes Article 27
options.D: there is no tension

questions.explanation: The passage states both provisions.

questions.question: In the Jordan Referral decision, the Appeals Chamber held that

options.A: head-of-state immunity bars the ICC
options.B: only the Security Council may arrest heads of State
options.C: Jordan was not bound by the Statute
options.D: there is no customary rule recognising head-of-state immunity before an international court, and States Parties must cooperate

questions.explanation: The passage states the holding.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct?

options.A: The crime of aggression is on the same footing as other crimes
options.B: India is not a party to the Rome Statute, though it may be affected where a situation is referred by the Security Council
options.C: The ICC has no jurisdiction over war crimes
options.D: India is a party to the Rome Statute

questions.explanation: The passage states India is not a party; Security Council referral extends jurisdiction to non-parties.

passages.title: Trade Marks, Well-known Marks and Pharmaceutical Patents
passages.passage: The Trade Marks Act, 1999 provides for the registration of marks capable of being represented graphically and distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others. Section 9 lists absolute grounds for refusal, such as marks devoid of distinctive character, and Section 11 relative grounds, including similarity to an earlier mark and the likelihood of confusion. Under Section 11(6), the Registrar must take into account factors in determining whether a mark is well known, including its knowledge in the relevant section of the public and its duration and extent of use. Section 29(4) protects a mark with a reputation against use of an identical or similar mark in relation to dissimilar goods where the use takes unfair advantage of, or is detrimental to, the mark's distinctive character or repute, a form of dilution. Where the mark is unregistered, the proprietor may bring an action for passing off, the elements of which are goodwill, misrepresentation and damage. In Amritdhara Pharmacy v. Satya Deo Gupta (1963), the Supreme Court said that the test of deceptive similarity is to be applied from the perspective of a person of average intelligence and imperfect recollection, and that the marks are to be compared as a whole. In Cadila Health Care v. Cadila Pharmaceuticals (2001), the Court held that stricter standards apply in cases of medicinal products, since the consequences of confusion between drugs may be harmful. In Toyota Jidosha Kabushiki Kaisha v. Prius Auto Industries (2018), the Court held that a mark's trans-border reputation may be protected even where it is not used in India, but that the claimant must show that the reputation had spilled over to India at the relevant time. The Patents Act, 1970 requires novelty, an inventive step and industrial applicability; Section 3(d) excludes the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance unless it results in enhanced efficacy, a provision explained in Novartis AG v. Union of India (2013), where the Supreme Court denied a patent to the beta crystalline form of imatinib mesylate. Section 84 permits the grant of a compulsory licence where the reasonable requirements of the public have not been satisfied, the invention is not available at a reasonably affordable price, or it is not worked in India; in Natco Pharma v. Bayer Corporation (2012), the first compulsory licence was granted for a cancer drug.

questions.question: The test of deceptive similarity in Amritdhara is applied from the viewpoint of

options.A: the proprietor of the mark
options.B: a judge
options.C: a person of average intelligence and imperfect recollection, comparing the marks as a whole
options.D: an expert in trade marks

questions.explanation: The passage states the test.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an element of passing off, as stated in the passage?

options.A: Misrepresentation
options.B: Goodwill
options.C: Damage
options.D: Registration of the mark

questions.explanation: The passage lists the three elements; registration is not required for passing off.

questions.question: In Cadila Health Care, a stricter standard was applied to medicinal products because

options.A: pharmaceutical companies are powerful
options.B: drugs are costly
options.C: confusion between drugs can have harmful consequences
options.D: the Act so provides for medicines alone

questions.explanation: The passage states the reason.

questions.question: In Toyota v. Prius, the claimant's trans-border reputation would be protected where

options.A: the reputation had spilled over to India at the relevant time
options.B: the mark is registered abroad
options.C: the mark is not used in India at all
options.D: the mark is famous anywhere in the world

questions.explanation: The passage states that the claimant must show spill-over.

questions.question: Section 3(d) of the Patents Act, as applied in Novartis, excludes

options.A: all chemical inventions
options.B: the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance unless it results in enhanced efficacy
options.C: inventions made abroad
options.D: all pharmaceutical inventions

questions.explanation: The passage states the rule and the outcome.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a ground for a compulsory licence under Section 84 as stated in the passage?

options.A: The invention is not available at a reasonably affordable price
options.B: The patentee refuses to sell to a competitor
options.C: The reasonable requirements of the public are not satisfied
options.D: The invention is not worked in India

questions.explanation: The passage lists the first three grounds only.

passages.title: Right to Property under Article 300A and Compulsory Acquisition
passages.passage: The Constitution (44th Amendment) Act, 1978 omitted the right to property from the list of fundamental rights, repealing Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, and inserted Article 300A, which provides that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law. The right to property thus ceased to be a fundamental right but remains a constitutional right. In Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat (1995), the Supreme Court held that Article 300A requires the deprivation to be by a valid law, and that the 'law' must be one which satisfies the standards of reasonableness. In K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011), the Court held that a law depriving a person of property must serve a public purpose, though the adequacy of compensation is not justiciable and the absence of a provision for compensation does not by itself invalidate the law; in certain cases, however, it may be necessary under Article 300A. In Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2020), the Court described the right to property as a human right and a constitutional right, and held that the State cannot take possession of private land without the authority of law, nor claim title by adverse possession against a citizen. In Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar Shaw (2024), a seven-judge Bench held that Article 300A contains certain procedural rights of the owner, which the State must observe before depriving him of property: the right to notice, the right to be heard, the right to a reasoned decision, the duty to acquire only for a public purpose, the right to fair compensation, the right to an efficient and expeditious process, and the right of conclusion, namely that the acquisition must be completed. The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (LARR Act) replaced the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Under Section 24(2), an acquisition initiated under the old Act lapses where, in the case of land acquisition proceedings, the award was made five years or more before the commencement of the 2013 Act, but physical possession was not taken or compensation was not paid. In Indore Development Authority v. Manohar Lal (2020), a Constitution Bench held that compensation is 'paid' where it is tendered, and that the deposit of compensation in the treasury is not by itself sufficient for the owner to be deprived; and that the lapse requires both failures, possession and payment, together.

questions.question: After the 44th Amendment, the right to property is

options.A: a Directive Principle
options.B: a constitutional right under Article 300A, though not a fundamental right
options.C: a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(f)
options.D: abolished

questions.explanation: The passage so states.

questions.question: In K.T. Plantation, the Supreme Court held that

options.A: the right to property is a fundamental right
options.B: compensation must always be adequate
options.C: a law depriving property must serve a public purpose, though the adequacy of compensation is not justiciable
options.D: property can be taken without any law

questions.explanation: The passage records this holding.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the procedural rights recognised in Bimal Kumar Shaw?

options.A: Right to notice
options.B: Right to be heard
options.C: Right to a reasoned decision
options.D: Right to select the acquiring authority

questions.explanation: The last is not among the seven rights.

questions.question: Under Section 24(2) of the LARR Act, as interpreted in Indore Development Authority, an acquisition lapses where

options.A: compensation was deposited in the treasury
options.B: the owner objected
options.C: both physical possession was not taken and compensation was not paid, for the requisite period
options.D: either possession was not taken or compensation was not paid

questions.explanation: The passage states that the lapse requires both failures.

questions.question: Compensation is 'paid' within Section 24(2) when

options.A: it is announced in the award
options.B: it is deposited in the treasury
options.C: it is entered in the Government's accounts
options.D: it is tendered to the owner

questions.explanation: The Constitution Bench held that tender is sufficient for 'payment'; treasury deposit alone is not.

questions.question: In Vidya Devi, the Court held that the State

options.A: cannot take possession of private land without the authority of law, nor claim title by adverse possession against a citizen
options.B: may deprive land without notice
options.C: may claim title to private land by adverse possession
options.D: has absolute power over land

questions.explanation: The passage states this.

passages.title: Precedent, Ratio Decidendi and the Authority of the Supreme Court
passages.passage: Article 141 of the Constitution provides that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India. The expression 'law declared' is taken to refer to the ratio decidendi of a decision, that is, the principle of law necessary for the decision on the material facts, and not to obiter dicta, which are observations made in passing; though the obiter dicta of the Supreme Court are entitled to great weight, they are not binding in the strict sense. Jurisprudence has differed on the nature of judicial decision. The declaratory theory, associated with Blackstone, holds that judges do not make law but discover and declare what the law already is. The opposing view, associated with Bentham and Austin, regards judge-made law as law made by the judges, and Austin called the common law 'judiciary law'. A decision is said to be per incuriam, and therefore not binding, where it is given in ignorance of a binding statute or of a binding authority of a superior court, as explained in Young v. Bristol Aeroplane Co. and applied in A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak (1988). A decision rendered sub silentio, without the point having been argued or considered, has no precedential value on that point. The doctrine of stare decisis promotes certainty, but the Supreme Court is not bound by its own decisions and may overrule them, for example in Golaknath, where it applied prospective overruling to avoid disruption. In Central Board of Dawoodi Bohra Community v. State of Maharashtra (2005), the Court held that a Bench of coequal strength is bound by the decision of another Bench of the same strength, and that if it disagrees, it can only refer the matter to a larger Bench, which also applies to decisions of Constitution Benches, which a smaller Bench cannot doubt. Under the doctrine of merger, as explained in Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala (2000), when a superior court entertains an appeal and passes a decree, the decree of the lower court merges in that of the superior court. The Court's power under Article 142 to do complete justice is not a licence to override statutory or constitutional prohibitions, and a curative petition, evolved in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002), permits a final judgment to be reconsidered in rare cases of a gross abuse of process or violation of natural justice, where a review has been dismissed.

questions.question: The 'law declared' within Article 141 refers to

options.A: the ratio decidendi of a decision
options.B: obiter dicta alone
options.C: every observation in a judgment
options.D: only the final order

questions.explanation: The passage states that it refers to the ratio decidendi.

questions.question: A decision given in ignorance of a binding statutory provision is

options.A: a decision sub silentio only
options.B: valid for lower courts only
options.C: per incuriam, and not binding
options.D: binding as a precedent

questions.explanation: The passage states this.

questions.question: The declaratory theory of Blackstone holds that

options.A: the legislature is subordinate to judges
options.B: judges discover and declare the existing law
options.C: judges make new law
options.D: precedent has no value

questions.explanation: The passage states this.

questions.question: A two-judge Bench disagrees with a decision of a Constitution Bench. In accordance with Dawoodi Bohra, it should

options.A: ignore the decision
options.B: overrule the Constitution Bench
options.C: refer the matter to a larger Bench, since a smaller Bench cannot doubt a Constitution Bench
options.D: decide as it prefers

questions.explanation: The passage states that the smaller bench can only refer the matter to a larger Bench.

questions.question: A curative petition is permitted

options.A: in rare cases of gross abuse of process or violation of natural justice, after the dismissal of a review
options.B: only in criminal cases
options.C: whenever a party loses
options.D: as a second appeal

questions.explanation: The passage states the position.

questions.question: Consider the following. 1. Obiter dicta of the Supreme Court are binding in the same manner as ratio. 2. A decision sub silentio has no precedential value on the point not argued. 3. The Supreme Court may overrule its own earlier decisions. Which are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 2 and 3 only
options.C: 1 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Obiter dicta are weighty but not strictly binding; statements 2 and 3 are accurate.
